messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Esperanza is a 74-year-old Latin American woman who has worked as a pharmacist for nearly four decades, a career she built with quiet discipline and a deep sense of purpose. She is married — her second marriage, to a man she describes as gentle — and she came to the intake appointment dressed neatly, speaking in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart when she reached certain words. Her PCL-5 score of 66 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions is one of a woman whose interior life has been reshaped, almost architecturally, by years of physical abuse at the hands of her first husband.

The abuse spanned nearly a decade. What Esperanza returns to most often is not a continuous narrative but a series of frozen images: herself pressed against the kitchen wall, his hand raised; the particular angle of light through a window the moment a door slammed open and she knew what was coming; the sound of footsteps in the hallway, the specific creak of a hinge. She describes remembering the events not as a story she can tell from beginning to end but as a handful of vivid stills, each one complete and unbearable — a snapshot quality that means the past never quite recedes into sequence. More distressing still, when these images surface, she does not only see them. She feels her shoulders curl inward, her arms draw up, her body returning without her permission to the posture of someone bracing for a blow. The memories carry a physical signature that belongs to then but arrives in now, and when they come, her body floods with shame — not anger at what was done to her, but a deep, mortifying sense that she allowed it, that she was the kind of woman to whom such things happened.

It is this shame, and the beliefs it has calcified into, that now organise so much of Esperanza's daily life. She has come to believe she is no longer the competent, capable woman who counselled patients for decades; that person, she feels, would not have endured what she endured. She has lost whatever faith she once held in people and in the order of things. Most corrosively, she has settled into a conviction that she is simply weak — and it is this belief that makes her most afraid of what other people might see if they got close enough to look. The appraisal of weakness functions almost as a standing instruction: do not let anyone near enough to confirm it. So she avoids people, deflecting invitations from colleagues at the pharmacy where she still works part-time, keeping conversations transactional. When a patient lingers to chat, or a coworker asks how she is doing with the warmth of someone who genuinely wants to know, Esperanza feels the approach as a kind of exposure and steps back — literally, sometimes, moving behind the dispensing counter. The belief in her own weakness also makes her afraid of her own emotional interior; she suppresses strong feeling with the vigilance of someone managing a hazardous substance, and she has learned not to look at herself in mirrors or to attend to her body in any deliberate way, because her body still feels like the site of her humiliation.

These avoidances, which seemed at first like reasonable self-protection, have over time reinforced the very beliefs they were meant to shield her from. Because she never allows herself to feel, she has no evidence that she could survive feeling. Because she keeps people at a distance, she has no experience of being known and not found wanting. The isolation has made the pharmacy feel smaller; she has reduced her hours twice in the past year, telling her husband it is because of her age.

The threat system that was shaped during the abuse has never fully deactivated. Inside her own home — the home she shares with a kind man — Esperanza listens for the sound of doors. When one opens or slams, her body goes rigid before her mind catches up, and the alarm her nervous system sounds pulls a memory forward, which sharpens the sense of danger, which makes her scan for the next sound. A comment from her husband about family — her children from her first marriage, her estrangement from a sister — lands as a trigger because the family she came from is woven into the history of what happened to her, and the mention of it can collapse the distance between then and now in an instant. Someone moving toward her emotionally produces the same collapse: closeness itself has become a warning signal.

What finally brought Esperanza to seek help was a moment at the pharmacy three months ago. A patient — an elderly woman, frightened, asking questions about a new medication — reached across the counter and briefly touched Esperanza's hand. Esperanza froze, then excused herself to the back room, where she sat for twenty minutes unable to move. She told no one. But that evening she told her husband she thought something was wrong with her, and he found her the referral. What she is most afraid of, she said at the end of the first session, is that she is too old and too far gone for anything to change. What she is hoping for, said more quietly, is to feel like herself again — though she is no longer entirely sure who that was.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph establishes that triggering stimuli (e.g., sounds, touch, family mentions) causally lead to or activate Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about weakness or shame); triggers are linked to memory and threat but not directly to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., belief in her own weakness) causally sensitise or generate triggering stimuli; the beliefs drive avoidance but are not described as expanding or creating the set of triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., shame, belief in weakness) causally bring forward or activate her intrusive memories; memories are described as arising from triggers and threat cues, but not from the appraisals themselves.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph establishes that the activated threat/alarm state causally produces or reinforces Esperanza's negative appraisals; the threat system is described as pulling memories forward and driving scanning behaviour, but is not linked to generating the beliefs about weakness or shame.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's avoidance behaviours or safety behaviours causally create or expand her triggering stimuli; the vignette notes avoidance reinforces beliefs but does not describe it as producing new or broader triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
A comment from her husband about family — her children from her first marriage, her estrangement from a sister — lands as a trigger because the family she came from is woven into the history of what happened to her, and the mention of it can collapse the distance between then and now in an instant. Someone moving toward her emotionally produces the same collapse: closeness itself has become a warning signal.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And each time a trigger fires — the creak of a hinge, a hand extended across a counter, a reference to her children — the conclusion arrives with it, quiet and certain: this is what weakness looks like, this flinching, this inability to simply be present in an ordinary moment.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She has come to believe she is no longer the competent, capable woman who counselled patients for decades; that person, she feels, would not have endured what she endured. She has lost whatever faith she once held in people and in the order of things.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The belief in her own weakness had also, over time, expanded the territory of what felt dangerous: once she had accepted that she was the kind of woman to whom terrible things happened, almost any sign of closeness or unpredictability became a potential signal — a coworker's unexpected warmth, a door opening in a room where she had not expected anyone to be.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Most corrosively, she has settled into a conviction that she is simply weak — and it is this belief that makes her most afraid of what other people might see if they got close enough to look.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The conviction of weakness did not stay still; it kept pulling the memories forward, as though they were proof she needed to keep consulting — she would find herself back against the kitchen wall not only when something in the world summoned her there, but when the thought arrived on its own: you let this happen, and here is what it looked like.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The threat system that was shaped during the abuse has never fully deactivated. Inside her own home — the home she shares with a kind man — Esperanza listens for the sound of doors. When one opens or slams, her body goes rigid before her mind catches up, and the alarm her nervous system sounds pulls a memory forward, which sharpens the sense of danger, which makes her scan for the next sound.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living inside that alarm, day after day, had become its own kind of evidence: feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering — that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, that the vigilance was not a symptom but simply an accurate reading of who she had become.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Because she keeps people at a distance, she has no experience of being known and not found wanting. The isolation has made the pharmacy feel smaller; she has reduced her hours twice in the past year, telling her husband it is because of her age.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The avoidance had also drawn its own map around her: each room she slipped out of, each conversation she cut short, each shift she no longer worked had become a landmark she could not pass without the thought arriving — another place, another person, another ordinary thing that was no longer safe.
<<<END>>>
